'''Paul Marmet''', {{Post-nominals|country=CAN|OC|FRSC}} (20 May 1932 – 20 May 2005) was a Canadian physicist, inventor, author, and professor at [[Laval University]] in [[Quebec City]], Canada, who served as the President of the [[Canadian Association of Physicists]].

Marmet is notable for developing a novel high-resolution electron velocity selector, a [[scientific instrument]] which became widely used by scientists around the world.

==Inventions==
Early in his career, Marmet developed a high-resolution electron selector with his mentor [[Larkin Kerwin]], a scientific instrument for studying [[ion]]ic electronic states.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Marmet |first1=Paul |last2=Kerwin |first2=Larkin |title=An improved electrostatic electron selector |journal=Canadian Journal of Physics |url=https://www.nrcresearchpress.com/doi/pdf/10.1139/p60-084 |date=June 1960 |volume=38 |issue=6 |pages=787–796 |doi=10.1139/p60-084 |bibcode=1960CaJPh..38..787M |access-date=4 October 2020|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Along with a [[mass spectrometer]] Marmet developed, the novel instrument had an energy resolution superior to then-available instruments and has been used widely by scientists studying [[electron scattering]], which led to the discovery of enhanced [[vibration]]al excitation in [[nitrogen]] and of [[Feshbach resonance]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Biondi |first1=Manfred A. |last2=Herzenberg |first2=Arvid |last3=Kuyatt |first3=Chris E. |title=Resonances in atoms and molecules |journal=Physics Today |url=https://physicstoday.scitation.org/doi/pdf/10.1063/1.2995241 |date=October 1979 |volume=32 |issue=10 |pages=44–49 |doi=10.1063/1.2995241 |bibcode=1979PhT....32j..44B |access-date=4 October 2020|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Marmet |first1=Paul |last2=Kerwin |first2=Larkin |title=This Week's Citation Classic: Marmet P & Kerwin L An improved electrostatic electron selector |journal=Current Contents |url=https://garfield.library.upenn.edu/classics1987/A1987K744200001.pdf |date=23 November 1987 |issue=47 |page=20 |access-date=4 October 2020}}</ref>

==Research==
Using the Marmet-Kerwin electron selector, Marmet and his research group discovered [[atom]]ic and [[molecule|molecular]] states excited by [[electron impact]] but not by [[photon]]s, such as doubly excited states that disobey spectroscopic [[selection rule]]s. The group also found negative-ion [[resonance]]s in which the incident electron temporarily attaches to the target atom or molecule.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bolduc |first1=E. |last2=Quéméner |first2=J. J. |last3=Marmet |first3=P. |title=Autoionizing 2s<sup>2</sup>2p<sup>4</sup>3s3l States of Ne and Related Ne<sup>−</sup> Resonances |journal=Journal of Chemical Physics |date=1972 |volume=57 |issue=5 |page=1957 |doi=10.1063/1.1678515 |url=https://aip.scitation.org/doi/10.1063/1.1678515 |access-date=17 October 2020|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Valin |first1=M |last2=Marmet |first2=P |title=Atomic structures in Kr between 22 and 32 eV |journal=Journal of Physics B: Atomic and Molecular Physics |date=1975 |volume=8 |issue=18 |pages=2953–2967 |doi=10.1088/0022-3700/8/18/014 |bibcode=1975JPhB....8.2953V |url=https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/0022-3700/8/18/014/pdf |access-date=18 October 2020|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Career==
After receiving his physics [[BSc]] in 1956 and [[DSc]] in 1960 from [[Laval University]] and entering the Physics faculty as an assistant professor at his [[alma mater]] school in 1961, Marmet became a full professor in 1967 at age 34.<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://doi.org/10.1063/1.2915209 | doi=10.1063/1.2915209 | title=Marmet, Stoicheff head Canadian Association |journal=Physics Today | date=1982 | volume=35 | issue=8 | page=52 | url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Starting in 1967, he was director of the Laboratory for Atomic and Molecular Physics at Laval University, serving until 1982.

Between 1981 and 1982, Marmet served as President of the [[Canadian Association of Physicists]].

From 1983 to 1990, he was a senior researcher at the [[Herzberg Institute of Astrophysics]] of the [[National Research Council Canada]] in Ottawa. While there, Marmet helped the [[University of Ottawa]] modernize its Physics education program.<ref name="about">{{cite web|last=Marmet|first=Paul|title=About the Author|url=https://www.newtonphysics.on.ca/info/author.html|work=Newton Physics|access-date=12 February 2013}}</ref>

In addition to the prominent role he played in developing the [[Canadian Space Program]], Paul Marmet also served on the executive committee of the [[CNSC|Atomic Energy Control Board of Canada]] (now the [[Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission]]).

==Opposition to quantum mechanics, relativity, and the Big Bang==
In his later years, Marmet became an outspoken critic of the [[Copenhagen Interpretation]] of [[quantum mechanics]], the [[theory of relativity]], and the [[Big Bang]] cosmological model. He maintained a website devoted to his view.<ref>{{cite web|last=Marmet|first=Paul|title=Newton Physics|url=http://www.newtonphysics.on.ca}}</ref>

Marmet was one of 34 signers of [https://cosmology.info/org/open-letter-on-cosmology.html ''An Open Letter to the Scientific Community''] advocating against the Big Bang cosmology.<ref name=OL>Lerner, Eric (2004) [https://www.newscientist.com/article/mg18224482-900-bucking-the-big-bang/ Bucking the big bang]. [[New Scientist]], 22 May.</ref>

He also held an opposing view on [[cosmological redshift]]<ref name=RedShift>Marmet, P. (1988) [https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1988PhyEs...1...24M/abstract A New Non-Doppler Redshift]. [[Physics Essays]] 1(1), 24.</ref> and advocated [[tired light]] cosmology.

==Activism==
In addition to his activities as a member of the first Associate Committee on [[Astronomy]] of the National Research Council since 1971 and his playing a crucial role in negotiations for the [[Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope]],<ref>[https://www.rasc.ca/paul-marmet Paul Marmet – Fellows Roster of the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada]</ref> Marmet was also promoting the development of [[Quebec]]'s first astronomical research [[telescope]].<ref name=OC/>
